Before jumping into the different meanings, here is the one idea that ties all of them together:

"Substance" always refers to what is real, actual, and fundamental — the real "stuff" of something, rather than its surface or appearance.

Keep this in mind. Every meaning of the word connects back to this central idea.
Meaning 1 — A Physical Material or Matter

This is the most everyday meaning. A substance is any physical material — something you can (at least in principle) touch, measure, or detect. It is simply a piece of matter with particular characteristics.

Examples:

  • Water is a clear, liquid substance.
  • Salt is a white, grainy substance.
  • The scientist found an unknown substance on the floor of the cave.
  • "What is this sticky substance on my hand?"

Think of it this way: if you can ask "what is this stuff made of?", the answer is likely a substance. It doesn't have to be a single chemical — it just has to be a physical thing with a distinct identity and qualities.

Substances can be solid, liquid, gas, or even plasma. They can be natural (wood, gold, water) or man-made (plastic, nylon, bleach).
Meaning 2 — The Real, Essential Content of Something

This is where the word moves away from physical matter and into ideas, speech, and writing. Here, substance means the actual meaning or core content of something — what it is truly about, stripped of decoration, style, or filler.

Think of it as the difference between a beautifully decorated empty box (no substance) and a plain box full of important things (full of substance).

Examples:

  • "His speech was very long, but it had no real substance." (= He talked a lot, but said nothing meaningful.)
  • "Let's get past the small talk and discuss the substance of the problem."
  • "The two politicians agreed on style but differed on substance." (= They may have spoken similarly, but their real ideas were very different.)
  • "Can you summarize the substance of the meeting for me?" (= Tell me what was actually discussed and decided.)

So when someone says "the substance of an argument," they mean the real point, the core claim — not how it was worded or presented.
Meaning 3 — Reality, Solidity, or Genuine Existence

This meaning is closely related to Meaning 2 but applies more broadly. When something has substance, it is real, credible, and grounded in fact or evidence. When something lacks substance, it is hollow, imaginary, or not backed by anything real.

Examples:

  • "There is no substance to these rumors." (= These rumors are not based on anything real.)
  • "The detective said the witness's story had substance." (= It seemed genuine and believable.)
  • "His promises turned out to have no substance." (= His promises were empty — nothing real behind them.)
  • "The ghost drifted through the wall — it had no physical substance." (= It had no real, solid, physical existence.)

You can also say something "gives substance to" a claim or idea, meaning it makes it more real or believable by providing evidence or proof.
Meaning 4 — Wealth and Social Standing (formal, slightly old-fashioned)

In older or more formal English, a person "of substance" means a person of wealth, property, and social importance — someone who has real, solid material resources in the world.

Examples:

  • "He was a merchant of considerable substance." (= He was a wealthy, respected merchant.)
  • "She came from a family of substance." (= Her family was well-established and wealthy.)

You are less likely to hear this in everyday modern speech, but you will encounter it in literature and formal writing.
Meaning 5 — A Drug or Chemical That Can Affect the Body or Mind (common in health and legal contexts)

In medical, legal, and social contexts, substance is widely used to refer to any chemical — especially a drug, alcohol, or controlled chemical — that a person might take into their body, and which can alter how they feel, think, or behave.

Examples:

  • "He was treated for substance abuse." (= He had a problem with drugs or alcohol.)
  • "The athlete tested positive for a banned substance."
  • "Controlled substances" (= drugs whose use, sale, and possession are regulated by law)
  • "She is recovering from a substance use disorder."

Here, the word is almost always either neutral or clinical in tone — it is often used deliberately instead of words like "drug" or "alcohol" to speak more broadly or professionally about the topic.
Meaning 6 — The Fundamental Nature of a Thing (philosophical)

In philosophy, substance carries a very specific and important meaning. It refers to the underlying, independent reality that makes a thing what it is — the fundamental "stuff" of existence itself, which exists on its own and doesn't depend on anything else to exist.

For example, philosophers have debated for centuries: Is the universe made of one substance (matter), or two (matter and mind), or many? Aristotle used "substance" to describe the basic essence of an individual thing. René Descartes famously argued that there are two substances in the world — the mind and the body — which sparked centuries of debate.

You don't need to go deep into philosophy to use the word, but knowing this meaning helps you understand why "substance" carries such weight. It has always meant the real thing itself, at the deepest level.

• "In substance" — meaning "essentially" or "in the most important way." "The two reports differ in details, but are the same in substance."
  • "Substance over form" — a phrase (common in law and business) meaning that what really matters is the true nature of something, not how it appears on paper.
  • "A person of substance" — someone important, credible, and serious (or, in the older sense, wealthy).
  • "Lack substance" — to be empty, shallow, or not backed by evidence.
  • "Substance abuse" — the harmful or addictive use of drugs or alcohol.
  • "Give substance to" — to make something more real, believable, or solid. "The new evidence gave substance to her claims."

Here's the thread running through every single meaning:

MeaningWhat is "real and fundamental" here?
A physical materialThe actual matter itself — the real stuff
Core content of speech/writingThe real meaning, not the surface presentation
Credibility and realityWhether something truly exists or is just an illusion
WealthReal, solid material resources
DrugsReal chemical agents that cause real effects on the body
PhilosophyThe deepest, most fundamental nature of reality

In every case, substance points inward, toward what is truly there. Its opposite is always something hollow, surface-level, fake, or unreal.
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine someone cuts through all the noise, decoration, and appearance of something and asks:

"But what is actually there? What is this really made of? What does this really mean?"

Whatever the answer to that question is — that is the substance.
